title: Free Verse
objective: After this level you can explain how free verse builds rhythm without regular meter or rhyme.
summary: Free verse drops regular meter for the cadences of speech but keeps the line. Its rhythm comes from patterned sounds, words and phrases, like Whitman's repetitions.

cards.headline: Compose to the musical phrase, not the metronome.
cards.body: That was Ezra Pound's advice to poets: "to compose in the sequence of the musical phrase, not in sequence of a metronome." Level 32's meter ticks along beat after even beat. Pound wanted poems that moved like music instead. Fine slogan. But without a fixed beat, where does the rhythm come from?

cards.headline: Free, not formless
cards.body: Free verse is poetry without a regular meter or set form, shaped instead by the cadences of speech. The name translates the French vers libre, a movement that began in France in the 1880s. Free doesn't mean shapeless, though. Free verse keeps the line, and uses it to set itself apart from prose. Level 31's line breaks still do their work.

cards.headline: Rhythm from repetition
cards.body: Instead of counting syllables, free verse patterns bigger things: sounds, words, phrases, whole sentences. Walt Whitman, the founding father of American free verse, opens Song of Myself: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume." Hear the echoes? Myself, myself. Assume, assume. The repetition is doing the metronome's job.

cards.fact: Free verse has very old roots.
cards.context: One of its greatest ancestors is the poetry of the Psalms and the Song of Songs in the King James Bible. Their parallel lines and sweeping repetitions follow Hebrew cadences, and they inspired poets from William Blake to Whitman. So the "new" freedom of free verse was, in part, a very old sound.

questions.prompt: How does free verse build rhythm without a regular meter?

options.label: By patterning sounds, words and phrases, often through repetition
By counting exactly ten syllables a line
By rhyming every pair of lines
By writing in paragraphs like prose

questions.explanation: Free verse rhythms come from patterned sounds, words, phrases and sentences, like Whitman's repeated "myself."

questions.prompt: Pound set free verse against "the metronome." From Level 32, what regular beat does the metronome stand for?

options.label: The rhyme at the end of each line
options.rationale: A metronome keeps time, not rhyme.

options.label: Meter: a measured pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables
The cutting word in a haiku
options.rationale: That's a pause, not a steady beat.

questions.explanation: Meter measures a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, the steady tick Pound wanted to escape.
